query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer (primarily Cr2O3) along grain boundaries and at the coating–substrate interface, which passivates the surface and mitigates abrasive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate in its as-deposited, equiatomic state with a baseline grain size.
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal pre-oxidation treatment in air (for example, holding the coating at 450°C for 1 hour) prior to high-temperature wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear testing performed in the 400–600°C range under controlled mechanical loads that simulate the intended service environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine, contiguous Cr-rich oxide layer (primarily Cr2O3) that localizes along grain boundaries and interfacial regions.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated selective oxidation of Cr leads to the development of a passivating oxide scale that protects the underlying metallic phases from direct abrasive interaction. This improved oxidation kinetics at grain boundaries, potentially supported by mesoscale simulations of oxygen diffusion, reduces the effective contact area during wear, thereby lowering both the wear rate and friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidation treated coatings will exhibit a lower wear rate and reduced coefficient of friction compared to as-deposited coatings, accompanied by clear evidence (via microscopy and phase analysis) of a continuous, protective Cr-rich oxide layer.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating without any thermal pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: Testing is valid within the temperature range of 400–600°C and under mechanical loads representative of the intended high-temperature service conditions, ensuring the coating remains in thin-film protective mode.
generation.uncertainty: The exact contributions of the individual alloying elements (e.g., whether additional elements like Cu play any secondary role in oxidation behavior) and the detailed kinetics of the oxide formation remain to be fully quantified, necessitating further combined experimental and simulation studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on identical conventional metal substrates. Subject one set to a thermal pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., 450°C for 1 hour in air), while keeping the second set as the untreated baseline. Perform high-temperature wear tests at 500°C under identical controlled loading conditions. Compare the wear rates, coefficients of friction, and oxide layer characteristics between both sets using microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and profilometry.
measurements: Wear rate (material loss per unit distance or time)
Coefficient of friction during sliding wear
Phase and thickness of the oxide layer (via XRD and SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidation treated coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction, and if phase analysis fails to reveal a continuous protective oxide layer relative to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
